newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian stores Nama expect HRK5 mln profit in '97.
newsitem.headline: Croatian stores Nama expect HRK5 mln profit in '97.

text.p: Zagreb-based department store chain NAMA said on Wednesday it hoped for a sales increase this year that may bring it a first profit after a series of losses during the war years.
"We expect sales of 800 million kuna this year," director Marija Sola told Reuters. "Net profit won't be very big, around five million kuna."
Nama, in which ailing Privredna Banka has a 41.5-percent stake, had a loss of 29.5 million kuna in 1996 despite sales of 700 million.
But apart from operating costs, it had to settle almost 47 million kuna in financing costs and other unplanned expenditures dating back to previous years, Sola said.
The 1996 loss was still cut down to about one third of those in previous years, plagued by poor sales.
The company now has 17, mostly sad-looking department stores with its Vukovar outlet in Eastern Slavonia completely destroyed. Of the rest, 12 are in the capital and the rest in other major towns.
It is to invest around 36 million kuna this year in refurbishing two main outlets at prime positions in the centre of Zagreb which account for some 60 percent of all sales.
"These plans were set back a little due to bank guarantees being late... You can imagine what it is doing to sales," Sola said, adding the stores should be reopened in the summer.
Among its plans for not so near a future, she mentioned rebuilding the Vukovar store from scratch once Eastern Slavonia is fully reintegrated under the government rule.

An additional worry to Nama are an estimated 400 surplus employees out of 2,670. But designs to lay off workers with severance in a bid to cut costs may be shelved due to strong opposition from the trade sector union, Sola said.
Before war broke out in Croatia in 1991, Nama had several foreign suitors, but it now seems to be in the dark as to what the future may bring in the way of privatisation.
Its own former and current employees control 27 percent of the equity, with the government holding around 33 percent through its pension funds and state privatisation agency.
"We don't know where these holdings will end up, it is for our owners to decide. We can only continue to work and hope for the best," Sola said. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
